title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
hook: a queen's strange illness, a cure no one could fetch, and a boy who rides home on a tigress

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa: a baby with a bell at his neck, found by the Pampa river and raised by the king of Pandalam as Manikandan. Did you stop for a small call for help? Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

The prescription is impossible on purpose. The queen of Pandalam lies in a darkened room, clutching her head. The palace physician bows and gives his verdict: only one cure will work, the milk of a tigress. The room goes silent. Nobody walks into the forest and milks a tiger. And the physician knows it. Because the illness, in the story, isn't real. It's a plan to send someone into the forest who isn't supposed to come back. Today, the boy who went anyway.
screen: `AN IMPOSSIBLE CURE` → `THE MILK OF A TIGRESS` → `AN ILLNESS THAT ISN'T REAL`

segments.voice: First, the fear behind the plan. In the telling, after the king adopts Manikandan, the queen has a son of her own. A scheming minister whispers to her that the adopted boy will take the throne from her child. Afraid, she agrees to pretend to be ill, and the physician is in on it. It's an old human fear, the kind that makes ordinary people do things they later regret. Second, the boy's answer. Manikandan is still young. He hears what the cure is, and he offers to go. The king begs him not to. The boy goes anyway, alone, into the forest, with a bundle of food for the road. The story doesn't make him angry, and it doesn't make him suspicious. He simply goes to fetch what his mother says she needs. Third, the return. In the forest, tradition says, Manikandan meets the demoness Mahishi and overcomes her, which was why he was born. And then he comes home. Not with a pot of milk, but riding on a tigress, with a band of tigers walking behind him. In some tellings the tigers are gods in disguise. The palace gate is full of terrified people. The queen and the minister, seeing him, understand what they've done, and they fall at his feet asking forgiveness. And the king finally understands who his son is. Notice where the story puts its weight. Not on punishment for the plotters, but on what the boy does with their plot: he turns a trap into an errand of care, and comes back with more than they asked for. Few errands today involve a tiger. But a task can still arrive that looks set up to fail.
screen: `A PLAN BORN OF FEAR` · `THE BOY GOES ANYWAY` · `HOME ON A TIGRESS` · `THE PLOTTERS ASK FORGIVENESS`

segments.voice: Walk into the forest for a while. Sit, and settle the breath. Bring to mind one task in front of you that feels set up to go badly: a hard meeting, a difficult conversation, a job nobody else wanted. Let yourself feel the weight of it. Then picture yourself setting out toward it calmly, a bundle on your shoulder, without resentment, without hurry. Breathe in steadiness. Breathe out suspicion. Stay with the picture of walking. If you pray, you can say Ayyappa's name softly with each breath. The bell holds the time.
Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, the tiger's milk: a cure meant as a trap, a boy who went anyway, and his return on a tigress. Today's word.
Your line: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, take one thankless task without complaint, and see what you bring back from it. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Ayyappa is often shown seated on or beside a tiger, and devotees retell how Manikandan went into the forest for tiger's milk and came home riding a tigress.

sources.ref: the Ayyappa story: the queen's feigned illness, the tiger's milk, the defeat of Mahishi, the return on a tigress
sources.work: Ayyappa tradition of Kerala (Pandalam and Sabarimala retellings)

notes: Kerala tradition, paraphrased; tellings vary. Confirm: the minister's role, the queen's own son, the bribed physician, Mahishi's defeat on the same journey, and the tigers as gods (Indra as the tigress in some tellings).
The queen is framed as acting from fear and then repenting, not as a villain. Keeper: confirm tone.
The original game uses व्याघ्री (tigress). Keeper: confirm spelling and whether a Malayalam word would be better here.
